**Narrative**

The most strongly perturbed pathway is **Galactose Metabolism** (KEGG map00052), which achieves a perfect FDR of 0.0 with a fold-enrichment of ~951 across six matched compounds. This finding is mirrored in the associated disease module **Galactosemia** (SMP00182, FDR=0.0), indicating that the observed metabolite signature recapitulates the biochemical hallmark of galactose-handling disorders.

The strongest drivers of this enrichment are **galactitol (C01697)**, **galactinol (C01235)**, and **sucrose (C00089)**, all of which are confirmed members of KEGG map00052. Galactitol, the alcohol reduction product of galactose, sits downstream of the canonical Leloir pathway; the KEGG reaction graph confirms a bidirectional path from **D-glucose (C00221)** to galactitol through five intermediates (UDP-glucose → UDP-galactose → galactose), establishing glucose as the upstream precursor. **Galactinol** (the raffinose-family galactosyl donor) is connected to galactitol in just two reaction steps (galactose as the shared intermediate), making it a proximal upstream driver of galactitol accumulation. **Sucrose**, which enters the pathway upon inversion to its component hexoses, is likewise annotated to this module.

Secondary pathway enrichment in **glycerophospholipid biosynthesis** (WP2533, FDR=7.9×10⁻⁵) is driven by **ethanolamine (C00189)**, **myo-inositol (C00137)**, and **glycerol (C00116)**, suggesting concurrent perturbation of membrane-lipid metabolism and inositol signaling. A minor enrichment of **dopamine (C03758)** within broader biochemical pathways is also noted, though it is not the dominant signal.

Biologically, coordinated elevation of galactitol alongside galactinol and sucrose is consistent with a blockade or saturation in the Leloir pathway (galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase or UDP-galactose-4-epimerase step), causing galactose to be shunted toward galactitol via aldose reductase. When combined with altered myo-inositol and ethanolamine levels, this signature points toward a metabolic stress phenotype affecting both sugar homeostasis and phospholipid membrane dynamics — a pattern reported in galactosemia patient studies and in cellular models of galactose toxicity.
